Your job is to write the regression tests that pin that behaviour down, in `scipy/stats/tests/test_f2p_scipy__scipy_21700.py`: enough to have shown what was wrong or missing before the change, and to catch it if anyone undoes it. One test per behaviour the change settles separately -- as many as the change has, and no more. A test is whatever this project's runner collects: a function in some projects, a method on a test class in others. The briefing above says which, and a test the runner does not collect is not a test. Work out what the code does *now*, what it will do *after* the change, and assert the difference. That difference is the whole subject of the test -- not the surrounding function, and not some other property that happens to be broken at the same time. Not every pull request fixes a bug. A feature adds something that does not exist here yet; a refactor or a speed-up may change little that a caller can see. Look for what does change -- a result for some input, an error raised or no longer raised, a new argument or name that now works. A test that only checks that a private name exists tests the code's spelling, not its behaviour. Some changes are about a situation this container does not have: an optional package that is missing, another version of a library, another platform. Then create that situation inside the test -- for example with pytest's `monkeypatch`, by hiding a module (`monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, "name", None)`) or replacing a value -- and assert what the change does there. The report itself is not the subject. It describes a symptom somebody noticed; what you assert has to be the behaviour underneath it, not the wording of the complaint. What this pull request is about: --- Pull request #21700: ENH: `stats.Mixture`: add mixture distributions for new infrastructure #### What does this implement/fix? This adds `scipy.stats.Mixture`, a class for mixture distributions. *Update: Don't be scared by the line count; almost all of it is just movement of documentation.* ```python3 import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy.stats import Mixture, Normal vars = (Normal(mu=-1.2, sigma=1.1), Normal(mu=1.3, sigma=0.9)) weights = (0.4, 0.6) X = Mixture(vars, weights=weights) x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 300) plt.plot(x, X.pdf(x)) plt.hist(X.sample(10000), density=True, bins=30) plt.show() ``` #### Additional information Questions: - ~~What should the class be called?~~ People seem happy with `Mixture`. - ~~What should the arguments be called? Should the random variables and their probabilities be separate lists (as they are now) or, say, a list of tuples?~~ People seem happy with separate `components` (positional only) and `weights`. - ~~To avoid copy-pasting all the method documentation, I was thinking that this and `ContinuousDistribution` should be a subclass of a new superclass `StatisticalDistribution`, and method documentation would go there. Of course, there will be several other subclasses, like `DiscreteDistribution`, etc. Should that superclass be created in this PR or shall we do a separate PR and rebase this after that merges?~~ I'd like to add `_ProbabilityDistribution` in this PR. Thoughts: - There are many ways of making this more efficient at the cost of extra complexity. Let's keep this simple. - Currently this is only for distributions with scalar shapes (not arrays). Separate PR can extend to array shapes. - I remember a request for zero-inflated distributions. I'd like to enable this by creating a degenerate/Dirac continuous distribution in a follow-up PR. The obvious alternative is to wait until there is a discrete uniform distribution (which could have all its mass at zero). - When there are discrete distributions in the mixture, I suppose the PDF at the support values of the discrete distributions will be infinite? And perhaps this class should _also_ have a PMF method, and the PMF at values that are not in the support of a discrete distribution would be zero? - I'll probably want to test edge behavior with distributions that have finite support (but it doesn't really matter until these are public). - `mode` may not return the global maximum of the PDF.     """Test that Mixture can be instantiated with components and weights"""

    # Create components
    components = [Normal(mu=-1.2, sigma=1.1), Normal(mu=1.3, sigma=0.9)]
    weights = [0.4, 0.6]
    
    # This should work after the PR is applied
    mixture = stats.Mixture(components, weights=weights)

    assert len(mixture.components) == 2

    """Test that Mixture can compute PDF values"""

    components = [Normal(mu=-1.2, sigma=1.1), Normal(mu=1.3, sigma=0.9)]
    weights = [0.4, 0.6]
    mixture = stats.Mixture(components, weights=weights)
    
    # Test PDF computation at a few points

    pdf_vals = mixture.pdf(x)
    
    # Should return array of same shape as input

    # PDF values should be non-negative
